title: Addressing Irritating Behavior With Ask-Tell-Ask
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Notes post takes up the small, persistent irritants every leader meets, such as the colleague who talks over others, answers email in meetings or arrives late. It argues that these behaviors are too minor for a formal conversation and too persistent to ignore, so silence lets the irritation harden into relational distance. The proposed remedy is ASK-TELL-ASK, a feedback sequence borrowed from medical education: the leader asks for the person's own view, shares one specific observation, then asks for a response. The first Ask matters because people commit more deeply to conclusions they reach themselves, while the Tell fills a blind spot rather than delivering a verdict. The second Ask returns ownership to the person, and the whole exchange can take two or three minutes. The piece concludes that handled lightly and early, small annoyances stay small.
points: Persistent minor irritants should be raised early and lightly, because saying nothing lets irritation grow into relational distance.
The sequence is Ask (a genuine question, not a disguised hint), Tell (one specific, observable example), then Ask again (invite the person's response).
The Tell is meant to fill a blind spot, not hand down a verdict, and one example is enough before the leader stops talking.
The approach keeps the person in charge of their own conclusion, which makes the feedback more likely to stick even when it seems not to land at first.
quotes: Annoying or irritating behaviors feel too small for a formal conversation, yet too persistent to ignore. Leaders who say nothing allow the irritation to grow, often causing relational distance.
In this sequence, the leader invites the person’s own view first, shares one specific observation, and then asks for the person’s response.
The first Ask rests on a well-established finding. People commit more deeply to conclusions they reach themselves.
Quite frequently, the first Ask surfaces very little. People are often unaware of what they are doing that annoys others. That is why the Tell matters.
For the interrupter, the Tell might be, “In Thursday’s planning meeting, you jumped in twice before one of your colleagues finished. They never got back to their point.
The person is never ambushed, is never asked to guess what the leader is thinking, and is never labeled.
Most annoyances don’t need a confrontation. They just need a question, an observation, and another question to resolve them.
context: Small irritants are awkward to raise, and ignoring them damages working relationships.
The method hands the person the first word so they can name the problem themselves.
Self-reached conclusions drive deeper commitment, which is why feedback opens with a question.
The Tell exists because people rarely see their own annoying habits.
A single concrete, dated example makes the observation specific instead of a label.
The conversation is kept light, brief and free of ambush or labeling.
The closing claim is that early, modest questions beat confrontation.
